name: Core: IP Services
description: 25 original questions for IP Services (10% of the v1.1 blueprint).
author: CCNA Academy

questions.stem: Arrange the DHCP messages exchanged when a client first obtains an address.
questions.explanation: The client broadcasts Discover, servers reply with Offer, the client broadcasts Request for one offer, and the chosen server confirms with Ack.
questions.whyCorrect: Discover → Offer → Request → Acknowledge

questions.stem: Clients in VLAN 10 (gateway R1 Gi0/1, 10.1.10.1/24) receive no IP address. The DHCP server is 10.0.0.50, reachable from R1 through Gi0/2. What fixes the problem?
questions.explanation: Routers do not forward broadcasts. 'ip helper-address' turns DHCP broadcasts into unicasts to the server and sets giaddr so the server picks the right pool.
questions.tip: Helper goes where the help is needed — the client side.
questions.whyCorrect: The relay must sit on the interface that receives the clients' broadcasts.
whyWrong: Gi0/2 faces the server and never receives client broadcasts.
Routers already route IPv4 by default; the problem is broadcast forwarding.
NAT does not relay DHCP broadcasts.

questions.stem: An IOS DHCP pool for 10.1.10.0/24 must never lease 10.1.10.1–10.1.10.20, and clients must receive gateway 10.1.10.1. Which commands achieve these two requirements? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: Typical pool: excluded-address (global), then 'ip dhcp pool NAME' with network, default-router, dns-server and lease.
questions.whyCorrect: This global command keeps the range out of every pool. This gives clients their default gateway.
whyWrong: This configures a relay, not the pool.
This sets the DNS server option, not the gateway.
The pool's network command uses a subnet mask or prefix length, not a wildcard.

questions.stem: True or false: A DHCP Discover is broadcast because the client has no IP address yet and does not know the server's address.
questions.explanation: The Discover is sent from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 (UDP 68 to 67). A relay is needed when the server is on another subnet.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. The Discover is sent from 0.0.0.0 to 255.255.255.255 (UDP 68 to 67). A relay is needed when the server is on another subnet.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which DNS record type maps a hostname to an IPv6 address?
questions.explanation: Common records: A (IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias), MX (mail), PTR (reverse), NS (name server).
questions.whyCorrect: AAAA records hold 128-bit IPv6 addresses.
whyWrong: A records hold IPv4 addresses.
PTR records map addresses back to names.
MX records identify mail servers for a domain.

questions.stem: Which statement about DNS transport is correct?
questions.explanation: DNS is a classic 'both' protocol: UDP for small query/response exchanges, TCP for zone transfers and large answers.
options: Queries use UDP 53; zone transfers use TCP 53
DNS uses only TCP 53 for every query
DNS uses UDP 67 for queries and replies
DNS uses only TCP 443 for all lookups
questions.whyCorrect: TCP is also used when responses are too large for UDP.
whyWrong: Most queries use UDP for speed.
UDP 67 belongs to DHCP servers.
DNS over HTTPS exists, but standard DNS uses port 53.

questions.stem: Match each NAT term to its definition.
questions.explanation: Inside/outside describes where the host is; local/global describes which side of the router the address is seen from.
questions.whyCorrect: Inside local → The real IP address of an inside host, usually private; Inside global → The public address that represents an inside host to the outside; Outside global → The real IP address of an outside host; Outside local → The address of an outside host as seen from the inside network
right: The real IP address of an inside host, usually private
The public address that represents an inside host to the outside
The real IP address of an outside host
The address of an outside host as seen from the inside network

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. What is the inside global address and port for PC2's session?
questions.explanation: In the translation table, the inside global column shows how an inside host appears on the internet.
questions.whyCorrect: PC2's private socket 192.168.1.11:51000 is translated to the shared public address on port 51001.
whyWrong: This is PC2's inside local address.
This is the outside global address of the web server.
This translation is already used by PC1.

questions.stem: Refer to the diagram. Why did the router change PC2's source port from 51000 to 51001?
questions.explanation: PAT identifies sessions by public IP + port. When two inside hosts use the same source port, PAT assigns a different one.
options: To keep each PAT translation unique
Because port 51000 is reserved on the internet
Because the web server requires odd port numbers
questions.whyCorrect: PAT changes the source port when needed to avoid collisions.
whyWrong: PAT keeps the original port when it is free.
51000 is an ordinary dynamic port.
Servers do not impose such requirements.

questions.stem: No translations appear after this configuration. Gi0/0 is the LAN (192.168.1.1/24) and Gi0/1 faces the ISP. What is wrong?
questions.exhibit:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 192.168.1.1 255.255.255.0
 ip nat outside
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 203.0.113.2 255.255.255.252
 ip nat inside
!
access-list 1 permit 192.168.1.0 0.0.0.255
ip nat inside source list 1 interface GigabitEthernet0/1 overload
questions.explanation: Mark interfaces correctly, then verify with 'show ip nat translations' and 'show ip nat statistics'.
options: The ACL wildcard mask is incorrect
questions.whyCorrect: The LAN must be 'ip nat inside' and the ISP-facing interface 'ip nat outside'.
whyWrong: 0.0.0.255 correctly matches 192.168.1.0/24.
'overload' is present.
PAT can overload the outside interface address.

questions.stem: Web server 192.168.1.10 must always be reachable from the internet at 203.0.113.10. Which NAT type is appropriate?
questions.explanation: Configure: ip nat inside source static 192.168.1.10 203.0.113.10.
questions.whyCorrect: A permanent one-to-one mapping allows inbound connections at any time.
whyWrong: Pool mappings exist only while the inside host has an active session.
PAT mainly supports outbound sessions; inbound access needs static mappings.
A private address is not routable on the internet.

questions.stem: True or false: Dynamic NAT without overload can run out of addresses when more inside hosts need translation than the pool contains.
questions.explanation: Each inside host needs its own pool address. When the pool is exhausted, new translations fail until entries time out — which is why PAT (overload) is common.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is true. Each inside host needs its own pool address. When the pool is exhausted, new translations fail until entries time out — which is why PAT (overload) is common.
whyWrong: The statement is true, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: A router synchronizes its clock to an NTP server that reports stratum 2. What stratum does the router report?
questions.explanation: Lower stratum means closer to the reference source. Each hop adds one.
questions.whyCorrect: A client is one stratum further from the reference clock than its server.
whyWrong: The router cannot share its server's stratum.
Stratum 1 servers are directly attached to a reference clock.
Stratum 0 is the reference clock itself (GPS or atomic).

questions.stem: During an incident review, syslog timestamps from different switches do not line up. What should be implemented?
questions.explanation: Configure 'ntp server <ip>', set the time zone, and add 'service timestamps log datetime msec'.
questions.whyCorrect: A common time source makes logs from different devices comparable.
whyWrong: SNMP monitors devices; it does not synchronize clocks.
Severity filters messages; it does not fix timestamps.
CDP discovers neighbors and does not set time.

questions.stem: Which statements about SNMP are correct? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: SNMP: manager ↔ agent, data organized in MIBs and identified by OIDs. Use SNMPv3 for security.
options: SNMPv3 can provide both authentication and encryption
Traps must be acknowledged by the manager
questions.whyCorrect: Get/Set requests go to the agent on port 161. The authPriv security level adds privacy (encryption).
whyWrong: Traps are unacknowledged; Informs are acknowledged.
v1 and v2c send community strings in clear text.

questions.stem: A router logs '%OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 on Gi0/1 from LOADING to FULL'. What is the severity of this message?
questions.explanation: Syslog format: %FACILITY-SEVERITY-MNEMONIC. Severities: 0 Emergency, 1 Alert, 2 Critical, 3 Error, 4 Warning, 5 Notification, 6 Informational, 7 Debugging.
questions.whyCorrect: The number between the dashes is the severity; 5 = Notification.
whyWrong: Warning is level 4.
The message shows 5, not 3.
Informational is level 6.

questions.stem: With 'logging trap warnings' configured, which messages are sent to the syslog server?
questions.explanation: Lower number = more severe. 'logging trap 4' sends Emergency, Alert, Critical, Error and Warning.
questions.tip: Every Awesome Cisco Engineer Will Need Ice cream Daily (0–7).
questions.whyCorrect: Choosing a level includes it and every more severe (lower-numbered) level.
whyWrong: A logging level is a threshold, not a single level.
Higher numbers are less severe and are excluded.
Notification, Informational and Debugging are filtered out.

questions.stem: Arrange the syslog severity levels from most severe (0) to least severe (7).
questions.explanation: Syslog severities run from 0 (Emergency) to 7 (Debugging).
questions.whyCorrect: Emergency → Alert → Critical → Error → Warning → Notification → Informational → Debugging

questions.stem: Which DSCP marking is recommended for voice bearer traffic?
questions.explanation: DSCP is 6 bits in the IP header. Voice is marked EF so every hop can give it priority queuing.
questions.whyCorrect: Expedited Forwarding is designed for low-delay, low-jitter traffic such as voice.
whyWrong: AF41 is commonly used for interactive video.
CS1 is commonly used for low-priority scavenger traffic.
0 is default best effort.

questions.stem: An ISP drops traffic above the contracted 50 Mbps. What should the customer configure outbound to avoid those drops?
questions.explanation: Providers commonly police; customers shape to match. Shaping adds delay but avoids drops.
questions.tip: Police stop you; shapers make you wait.
questions.whyCorrect: Shaping buffers bursts and sends them at the contracted rate.
whyWrong: Policing drops the excess itself — the same result as the ISP's drops.
WRED manages queue depth; it does not hold traffic to a rate.
Marking alone does not limit the sending rate.

questions.stem: Which statements describe Low Latency Queuing (LLQ)? (Choose two.)
questions.explanation: LLQ = CBWFQ (bandwidth guarantees per class) plus a policed strict-priority queue.
options: It provides a strict-priority queue for delay-sensitive traffic such as voice
The priority queue is policed so it cannot starve the other queues
It marks packets with DSCP values
It randomly drops packets before a queue fills
questions.whyCorrect: Priority traffic is always sent first. Traffic above the configured priority rate is dropped during congestion.
whyWrong: Marking is a separate QoS tool.
That is WRED.

questions.stem: Match each QoS tool to what it does.
questions.explanation: QoS tools work together: classify → mark → queue → avoid congestion → police/shape.
questions.whyCorrect: Classification → Identifies traffic by ACL, NBAR or existing markings; Marking → Writes a CoS or DSCP value into the header; Queuing → Schedules packets on a congested interface; Policing → Drops or re-marks traffic that exceeds a rate; Shaping → Buffers excess traffic and sends it later
right: Identifies traffic by ACL, NBAR or existing markings
Writes a CoS or DSCP value into the header
Schedules packets on a congested interface
Drops or re-marks traffic that exceeds a rate
Buffers excess traffic and sends it later

questions.stem: True or false: QoS creates additional bandwidth on a congested link.
questions.explanation: QoS manages existing bandwidth by prioritizing, protecting and limiting traffic classes; it never adds capacity.
questions.whyCorrect: The statement is false. QoS manages existing bandwidth by prioritizing, protecting and limiting traffic classes; it never adds capacity.
whyWrong: The statement is false, so this choice is incorrect.

questions.stem: Which global command forces a Cisco device to accept only SSH version 2 connections?
questions.explanation: SSHv2 requires RSA keys of at least 768 bits; 2048 bits is recommended.
questions.whyCorrect: This disables SSHv1.
whyWrong: This is not valid syntax; 'transport input' controls which protocols are allowed on lines.
Key generation has no version option.
This is not valid IOS syntax.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares FTP and TFTP?
questions.explanation: Use TFTP only on trusted management networks for simple image and configuration copies.
options: FTP: TCP with login; TFTP: UDP without login
TFTP uses TCP 21 and FTP uses UDP 69
TFTP supports directory listings and FTP does not
questions.whyCorrect: TFTP (UDP 69) is minimal; FTP (TCP 20/21) has logins and directory operations.
whyWrong: The transports and ports are swapped.
Neither encrypts; use SCP or SFTP for encryption.
The opposite is true.
